title: Pandas Merge, Concat and Reshape: Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision of combining and reshaping DataFrames in pandas: merge join types, keys and suffixes, concat, melt and pivot, stack and unstack, and MultiIndex basics.

chapters.title: Merge Mental Model and Join Types
points: pd.merge(left, right, on='key', how='inner') works like a SQL JOIN: it matches rows by key values, not by position or index label.

inner keeps only keys present in both frames; left keeps every left row and fills right columns with NaN; right is the mirror image; outer keeps all keys from both sides, with NaN on the missing side.
Example: orders.merge(customers, on='cust_id', how='left') keeps all orders even when the customer is missing.
Duplicate keys multiply: 2 left rows with key A and 3 right rows with key A produce 6 rows, so row counts can silently grow.
Interview Point: What is the difference between an inner and a left join? How many rows come back from a merge when keys repeat on both sides? How do you find which rows had no match?

chapters.title: Join Keys, Suffixes and Validation
points: Key arguments: on= when both columns share a name, left_on= and right_on= when the names differ (both key columns stay in the result), left_index=True and right_index=True to join on the index.
df.join(other) merges on the index and defaults to a left join; pd.merge defaults to inner on shared column names.
Overlapping non-key column names get suffixes=('_x','_y') by default; pass suffixes=('_l','_r') for readable names.
validate='one_to_one' | 'one_to_many' | 'many_to_one' raises MergeError if the key uniqueness assumption fails; indicator=True adds a _merge column with values left_only, right_only or both.
Interview Point: How do you merge when key column names differ? How do you guard against accidental row explosion? How do you audit which rows failed to match?

chapters.title: Concat: Gluing Frames Together
points: pd.concat([a, b]) stacks along axis=0 (rows) and aligns columns by name; missing columns are filled with NaN.
axis=1 places frames side by side and aligns on the index; join='inner' keeps only the shared labels and join='outer' (the default) keeps all.
ignore_index=True rebuilds a clean 0..n-1 index; without it the original indexes repeat, so loc by label can return several rows.
keys=['a','b'] labels each source and builds a MultiIndex of the source and the original index.
Interview Point: When do you use concat instead of merge? Why does the index repeat after concatenating? What happens to columns that exist in only one frame?

chapters.title: Melt and Pivot: Wide vs Long
points: pd.melt(df, id_vars=['id'], value_vars=['q1','q2'], var_name='quarter', value_name='sales') turns wide into long: the listed columns become rows.
df.pivot(index='id', columns='quarter', values='sales') turns long into wide and raises ValueError if any index/column pair is duplicated.
pivot_table(..., aggfunc='sum', fill_value=0) aggregates duplicates and is the safe choice for real data; the default aggfunc is mean.
Example: melt, then groupby, then pivot_table is the standard reshape round trip for tidy data.
Interview Point: Why does pivot fail on duplicates while pivot_table does not? When is long format better than wide? How do you reverse a melt?

chapters.title: Stack, Unstack and MultiIndex Basics
points: stack() moves the innermost column level into the row index (wide to long), and unstack(level=-1) moves an index level into the columns (long to wide).
A MultiIndex is an index with several levels: build it with set_index(['a','b']) or groupby on several keys, and read it with df.loc[('a1','b1')] or df.xs('b1', level='b').
unstack() creates NaN where a combination is missing (use fill_value=0), and in pandas 3 stack() keeps NaN values (only older pandas dropped all-NaN rows by default).
reset_index() flattens a MultiIndex back into ordinary columns; sort_index() is required before slicing a MultiIndex range.
Interview Point: What is the difference between pivot and unstack? How do you select one level of a MultiIndex? Why does unstack introduce NaN?

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Merge, Concat and Reshape
points: Join rows by key: df.merge(o, on='k', how='inner|left|right|outer', suffixes=('_l','_r'), validate='1:1', indicator=True).
Join on index: df.join(o); different key names: left_on= with right_on=; combine rows or columns: pd.concat([a,b], axis=0|1, ignore_index=True, join='outer').
Wide to long: pd.melt(df, id_vars, value_vars, var_name, value_name); long to wide: pivot (unique pairs) or pivot_table (aggfunc, fill_value).
Level moves: df.stack() puts columns into the index, s.unstack(level) puts the index into columns; set_index and reset_index convert between columns and the index.
Interview Point: Which tool for which job (merge, join, concat, pivot_table, unstack)? Which checks do you run after a merge (row count, indicator, validate)?
